chunks.text: 3 Numerical Results We evaluate the capability of the proposed approach to super-resolve widefield fluorescence microscopy images, achieving resolutions smaller than the diffraction limit evaluated thanks to Argolight SIM slide. Our first results are on data simulated by means of the double-Poisson forward model ( 1 ). Next, we show the robustness of the proposed approach on real images of an ARGO-SIM pattern [ 5 ] . Simulated Argolight data. We simulate T = 500 T=500 frames of an ARGO-SIM calibration pattern consisting of 8 groups of 4 parallel lines. The centre-to-centre separation distance d d between the two inner lines increases progressively in steps of 30 nm 30\text{\,}\mathrm{nm} starting from 120 nm 120\text{\,}\mathrm{nm} . Fluorophore emission along the lines is modelled pixel-wise using a Poisson distribution with β = 1 \beta=1 and corrupted according to ( 1 ) with an under sampling factor r = 6 r=6 , Gaussian blur with FWHM = 311 nm \mathrm{FWHM}=$311\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}$ , and Poisson-Gaussian noise with α = 12 , σ = 5 \alpha=12,\sigma=5 . The corrupted frames have a final pixel size of 100 nm 100\text{\,}\mathrm{nm} . To quantitatively assess line separation, we computed the 1D intensity profiles of the reconstructions by summing pixel intensities along the direction of the lines and normalising them in the range [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . We evaluated our method on the simulated data and found optimal performance with regularisation weights λ 1 = 0.05 \lambda_{1}=0.05 and λ 2 = 40 \lambda_{2}=40 in terms of the peak-to-valley ratio of the profiles. We compare our results with those obtained with SACD [ 6 ] (using 20 initial and 100 final LR iterations and with the exact PSF) and eSRRF [ 5 ] (with radius R = 1 R=1 and sensitivity S = 1 S=1 ). As illustrated in Fig. 1 , our method successfully resolves the two inner lines down to the finest tested separation of 120 nm 120\text{\,}\mathrm{nm} , as also confirmed by the intensity profiles plot.

In contrast, under the tested configurations, eSRRF and SACD are only capable of resolving line pairs separated by at least 300 nm 300\text{\,}\mathrm{nm} and 240 nm 240\text{\,}\mathrm{nm} , respectively. Real ARGO-SIM.

Raw images, kindly provided by the authors of [ 5 ] , were acquired on a Carl Zeiss ELYRA PS.1 microscope equipped with an α \alpha Plan-Apochromat 100×/1.46 oil-immersion objective and an Andor EMCCD 887 1K camera [ 5 ] . A 128 × 128 128\times 128 pixel region of interest of the gradually spaced line pattern on the Argo-SIM calibration slide was recorded at 86 frames per second, yielding a sequence of T = 1000 T=1000 frames. The structure is identical to the one described above. The FWHM was estimated at 167 nm, while the noise parameters α \alpha and σ \sigma were derived through mean-variance curve fitting. We evaluated our method on these corrupted images using an upsampling factor of 2 2 . Setting the regularisation weights to λ 1 = 0.80 \lambda_{1}=0.80 and λ 2 = 60 \lambda_{2}=60 yielded optimal results in terms of the peak-to-valley ratio of the 1D intensity profiles, allowing us to resolve lines down to the minimum considered separation of 120 120 nm. Fig. 3 benchmarks our reconstruction against SACD and eSRRF. We performed SACD with 20 20 initial and 100 100 final LR iterations, setting the microscope numerical aperture and emission wavelength taken from the acquisitions metadata. eSRRF was run with R = 1 R=1 and S = 2 S=2 , following the recommendations of [ 5 ] . While eSRRF and SACD struggle to provide a clear and distinctly separated 1D intensity profile at 120 120 nm, our method produces visually sharper, distinctly isolated peaks with higher contrast and a significantly suppressed background noise. Furthermore, although SACD results in sharper lines than eSRRF, it introduces edge artifacts, thus hallucinating spurious lines at the boundaries. Figure 3: Real Argolight comparison. 4 Conclusions In this paper, we presented a physics-informed generative approach for fluctuation-based fluorescence microscopy super-resolution, combining flow matching techniques with model-based regularisation taking advantage of a double-Poisson problem describing the physical behaviour of the fluorophores and the whole image formation process. Experiments on both simulated and real Argolight data demonstrate promising resolving capabilities compared with the existing fluctuation-based approaches. Future work shall focus on the extension of the framework considered to accommodate non-static scenarios and photo-bleaching, alongside further validation on live-cell biological data. The code of the experiments reported in this work is available at: https://github.com/cozzalberto/flow_fluo
